articles.title: Open Canvas: A Free Open Source Infinite Canvas for Storyboarding, Film Planning and Visual Thinking
articles.excerpt: Most creative projects do not begin with a perfectly organized document. They begin with scattered ideas. A reference image here. A camera angle there. A rough scene description. A character concept.…
articles.body: Most creative projects do not begin with a perfectly organized document. They begin with scattered ideas. A reference image here. A camera angle there. A rough scene description. A character concept. A location photo. Maybe a few arrows connecting things that only make sense inside your head. Traditional documents are not particularly good at this kind of thinking. That is exactly the problem DJAI Open Canvas is trying to solve. DJAI Open Canvas is a free, open-source, local-first infinite canvas built for visual thinking, storyboarding, film pre-production, mood boards, diagrams and shot planning. Instead of forcing your ideas into pages, slides or rows, it gives you an open space where you can arrange information visually.

articles.title: Observer Pattern: eventi senza accoppiamento
articles.excerpt: Il problema dell'effetto domino Quando salvi un articolo, devi invalidare la cache. Quando cancelli un utente, devi eliminare le sue sessioni. Quando aggiorni un prezzo, devi ricalcolare i totali. Ogn…
articles.body: Il problema dell'effetto domino Quando salvi un articolo, devi invalidare la cache. Quando cancelli un utente, devi eliminare le sue sessioni. Quando aggiorni un prezzo, devi ricalcolare i totali. Ogni azione scatena reazioni — e la tentazione e infilare tutto nel metodo save() del modello, creando un metodo che fa dieci cose e ne conosce altrettante. E una violazione flagrante del Single Responsibility Principle : il modello dovrebbe occuparsi di persistenza, non di cache, notifiche e audit. L' Observer Pattern rompe questa catena causale diretta. Il modello non sa chi lo osserva e non gli interessa: sa solo che quando cambia il suo stato, deve notificare chi si e registrato.

articles.title: How the rankings work — and what we refuse to count
articles.excerpt: Positions in RSS Atlas are not for sale. There are ad slots, but they are separate, labelled "Ad", and take no part in the ranking calculation. Anyone can write that sentence, so here is what is actua…
articles.body: Positions in RSS Atlas are not for sale . There are ad slots, but they are separate, labelled "Ad", and take no part in the ranking calculation. Anyone can write that sentence, so here is what is actually counted — and, more importantly, what is deliberately not. The three signals Signal What it represents Favorites Someone decided they wanted to come back to it Page views The feed's detail page was opened AI fetches An AI tool retrieved the feed over MCP These are combined with time decay , so recent interest counts for more. A feed read heavily last year sits below one being read this week. The ordering is public : favorites weigh most, then views, then AI fetches. The coefficients and thresholds are not .

articles.title: [Claude Code in Practice] Rethinking Terminal Workflows: From zsh Autocomplete to Search and Diff Toolchains
articles.excerpt: Pain Point: Starting Over with Every Command When using Claude Code for tasks, there have always been two minor frictions that I hadn't seriously addressed until now. The first is that the shell itsel…
articles.body: Pain Point: Starting Over with Every Command When using Claude Code for tasks, there have always been two minor frictions that I hadn't seriously addressed until now. The first is that the shell itself is too bare-bones: there's nothing in ~/.zshrc except for two lines of PATH . No auto-completion, no command history. Navigating history requires pressing the up arrow repeatedly, and even then, similar commands must be manually edited. The second is when collaborating with Claude Code, some commands that are clearly read-only and have no side effects (listing files, checking versions, curling a README) require a manual "allow" click every time. This back-and-forth breaks the flow.

articles.body: Preface: It all started with a misunderstanding. I noticed a new page in the Gemini API documentation called Omni , introducing a model named Gemini Omni Flash, described as "natively multimodal, processing text, images, audio, and video simultaneously." My first thought was straightforward: if I throw a whole folder of videos and photos from my phone into it, let it understand what each asset is about, and then tell it in one sentence to edit them into a short video—isn't that a video editing app? articles.body: Can Venus cast a shadow? With Aug. 12's total solar eclipse — where the moon's dark silhouette is everything — now behind us, it's a good time to test another kind of celestial shadow. Astronomical folklore has it that the second rock from the sun, Venus , is, after the sun and moon, the third object able to cast a shadow when it's near peak brightness, albeit extremely faint, according to EarthSky . Is it true? Not in a city, where skylights glow and porch lights blaze, where shadows are mostly thrown by passing cars that appear to become the brightest object in the solar system briefly. articles.title: Water can survive surprisingly close to the Milky Way's supermassive black hole, James Webb Space Telescope finds
articles.excerpt: Water and cosmic dust can survive in the harsh environment near Sagittarius A*, new observations reveal.
articles.body: The heart of the Milky Way may be more hospitable to water than astronomers thought. Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers detected water and cosmic dust around an aging star only 0.55 light-years from Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy. The new study suggests that water and dust can form and survive surprisingly close to a supermassive black hole , where intense radiation and other harsh conditions might otherwise be expected to destroy them. The team used Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) to study IRS 3, an aging star located in the crowded environment surrounding Sgr A*, which has a mass of about 4 million suns, according to a statement from the European Space Agency (ESA). (Image credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, F.

articles.title: The Brink of War Review: Jeff Daniels and Jared Harris Lock Horns in Talky Cold War Drama
articles.excerpt: Read our review of The Brink of War, the Cold War political drama starring Jeff Daniels as Ronald Reagan and Jared Harris as Mikhail Gorbachev.
articles.body: The Brink of War is now playing in theaters. Writer-director Michael Russell Gunn’s well-meaning feature film debut, The Brink of War, takes a wordy, academic approach to chronicling the two momentous days in October 1986 when US President Ronald Reagan (Jeff Daniels) and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev (Jared Harris) sat across a table in a house in Reykjavik, Iceland hoping to strike a landmark nuclear disarmament deal designed to keep the Cold War from finally turning into a hot one. (Impressively, the film was shot at the actual location and in the same rooms where the leaders spoke.) As thoughtful and earnest as the drama is, it’s also pretty chill for a movie about trying to prevent nuclear war.

articles.excerpt: Ferrari rolled out a new one-off at Monterey called the CZ26, and the face of it looks a lot like the brand’s first electric car. Underneath, it’s an SF90 Stradale plug-in hybrid with a 7.9 kWh batter…
articles.body: Ferrari rolled out a new one-off at Monterey called the CZ26, and the face of it looks a lot like the brand’s first electric car. Underneath, it’s an SF90 Stradale plug-in hybrid with a 7.9 kWh battery and 25 km of electric range. So Ferrari built something that wears the Luce’s design language on top of a twin-turbo V8. Basically, what you’d get if the Luce and the SF90 had a baby.

articles.title: ISS photobombs the sun during solar eclipse | Space photo of the day for Aug. 14, 2026
articles.excerpt: The silhouette of the ISS transiting across the sun's face during the Aug. 12, 2026 total solar eclipse.
articles.body: The silhouette of the ISS transiting across the sun's face during the Aug. 12, 2026 total solar eclipse. (Image credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky) This week's total solar eclipse captured the world's attention, and millions of skywatchers looked up (with the correct protective eyewear, hopefully) to experience the moon blocking out our star's light. And, as you can see in this image, even the International Space Station (ISS) itself got in on the fun. What is it? On Aug. 12, 2026, the moon completely blocked out the sun's light for millions of lucky skywatchers witnessing a total solar eclipse. But the moon isn't the only thing orbiting Earth. Tons of satellites and probes do too, and that includes the ISS. This created a truly remarkable moment for some skywatchers.
